Shanghai, China.
Nov. 6, 1938
Dearest Kits:
So much to say I hardly know where to start. I left Nanking Wednesday at
six in a hire car with two Chinese passengers and one other foreign passenger and
two Chinese chauffeurs, each one nearly as big as Chillie Vaughn. It took us thirteen
and one half hours to make Shanghai.
It was
intensely interesting but I am sure
you would not have liked it, until you had got to Shanghai.
The road was narrow
all the way, rainy and misty most of the way. The road was fairly good some of the
way but muddy and rutty most of the way.
The two Chinese passengers spoke English
and were very nice. We were stopped many times by soldiers and questioned but never
delayed. We took a road running south of Wusiph on the south side of Tahu Lake
that comes in to the Shanghai Hangehow road about two or three miles from Minghong.
Of course all of such trips have abad reputation and Mr. Johnson will not give
authority for any one to make it. We skidded badly on one place where the road is
narrow and on top of a dyke about fifteen feet high and I thought we were going
over surely. We were, but fortunately the side of the car smashed into a tree
and helå us. The side of the car was badly smashed, glass broken, but far tunately
it was shatter proof, the door mas jammed, fender smashed and top
of car bent in,
but we didn't go over, and the frame of the chassis wasn't bent. We all got out,
got the car back in the road. I found out why the two big Chinese chauffeurs were
used, and we went on.
We had to run in low and second so much we boiled out most
of the water in the radiator and the engine got so hot it ran for five minutes with
the switch off. Finally stopped it by putting it in high gear with the brakes on.
We didn't have anything to get water in, dark as hell, but the car had one of the
old style
horns with a big rubber bulb about as big as your head so the chauffeur
took it off and sucked up water in it from a wayside ditch and squirted in the
radiator You can't beat the Chinese. We got stuck several times but managed to
push ourselves out.
We struck the ferry west of Minghong about five A.M. at daybreak. The
Terry came over, unloaded two new truck chassis and then turned around and went
back empty.
We inquired as to what in the hell was going on and were told that
there were
about thirty trucks on the other side going to kanking and the drivers
had parked their trucks all over the road on the other side and dow both the loading
and unloading runways so that it was impossible to unload anything on the other side.
Can you imagine anything more typical than that, more unbelievable? I immediately
decided that was no place for us.
We were only
about fifteen miles or less from
the Front and if the weather that day was good
all those new trucks standing there
would draw Jap planes like sugar drawing flies.
It took 35 minutes to make a round
trip on the ferry taking two trucks at a time and we were in for an eight hour wait.
I got our other passengers together and told them I thought we should cross outselves
on the Engłisixerex empty ferry going back and wait on the other side for our car
to get over.
There was no place to flop, no where to go, no protection at all and
in case of
attack it would have been a death trap. The other foreigner agreed at
once but the Chinese said the other side was like this side and we might loose our
baggage. I told nim I thought it was important to get over before flying started
and not get caught on the ferry, and once on the other side we could walk down the

road a mile and be away from the danger point.
case of attack that at least half of everynepresent would be killed and maybe
seventy-five percent;
that we would not have an even chance, and under such con-
ditions his baggage was nothing.
So they came with me. The other side was a
sight. Rule one on page one in Military Transport is to keep the roads unblocked
at any cost, but these damn fools were parked as tightly as possible all over the
road when they would have advanced their own cause by lining up properly on one
side of the road, and both ramps to the ferry were full. Fortunately for us the
first truck in line was a big army truck heavily loaded and guarded by six soldiers.
They had to go up about a 45 degree incline to get on the ferry and their truck
couldn't make it, so we helped them push and got them on.
I had passed around
cigarettes and they became very friendly and one of the Chinese passengers told
them our trouble. So they told us to come on and go back with them and they would
get us on the ferry. We asked them how were we going to get off on this side. They
said, "Sit on the ferry until these fellows back up and clear the road.
They can't
That made a hell of a lot of sense. to us and we piled
They were as good as their word and talked
turkey to the ferry official, moved our car up to the head of the line and put us
on •
Then the ferry official got cold feet and demanded that the soldiers go back
over and get us off. But the soldiers said they couldn't do that as they had to
hurry but for us to
stay on the ferry until we got off on the other side.
promised to do that. The ferry finally started back with much grumbling from the
Terry people. When we got over the drivers of the other side raised hell and re-
od the orior side retard not and re-
fused to move. We refused to go back and asked them to figure out the answer.
They finally backed up so we could get off and we went on our way rejoicing.
But
I looked back and all the trucks had scrambled back to their old positions and the
road and ferry landing was blocked again.
And I thought to myself "I hope all
you bastards get killed", the good old A.E.F. wise crack.
We got to Shanghai by
seven-thirty A.M.
The weather started raining and misting again so those half wits
got away with it as there was no flying that day.
The war my first day was very quiet and still is. If I could stay in
Shanghai I would bring you out. I see the papers talk of a terrific bombardment
but I don't know. Last night they shelled Lunghta from a point about north of our
house and not far away. You could trace the course of the shells by their sound
passing almost directly over our house. I couldn't figure it out until I saw this
morning that Lunghia had been shelled. I put chairs against the doors of our bed-
room to stop from them from rattling, but I slept o.K.
The Chinese certainly have been putting up a grand fight around here.
More power to them.
Everything at 279 is perfectly 0.K. Li and the coolie were on the job.
Amph came around and I gave her two months pay and told her to try to find another
job as I didn't know when you would be back. She said she would come back to you
when you did. I paid the house rent for Oct. and Nov. Bix paid it for Sept.
I
offered the house on a temporary basis to Karl Hill for $200.00.
That's all he
can pay. If
comes back and want it he will take it.
They will use their
own silver and linens. I am going to leave all our flat silver with Max Polin.
Phat isall I can do now. I must be back in Nanking wednesday. Ou outlook
(Company) is tough. There is a great deal of misunderstanding.
The most important
Chinese think we ran out on them. I have accomplished a little but not much
